cards.text: Psalm 125 is a song of ascents, and it's about people who trust in the LORD. The psalm says they're like Mount Zion. A whole MOUNTAIN, friend, and the closest I got to a mountain in that junk drawer was a stack of old takeout menus.

cards.question: What does the psalm say about Mount Zion that makes it a picture of people who trust the LORD?
The psalm says Mount Zion lasts only for a season.

cards.text: Jerusalem has mountains all the way around it, like a city with bodyguards made of solid ROCK. Try sneaking past THAT security with a fake badge.

cards.question: The mountains surround Jerusalem. In the same way, who surrounds the LORD's people?
How long does the psalm say the LORD surrounds His people?

answers.text: As long as the city stands

cards.text: Next the psalm brings up two things: the scepter of the wicked and the land allotted to the righteous. Me holding a scepter? I'd wrap my mustache around it and knock my OWN hat off.

cards.question: The psalm says the scepter of the wicked will rest on the land allotted to the righteous.
Why won't the scepter of the wicked rest on the land allotted to the righteous?

answers.text: So the righteous won't turn to injustice
So the righteous can grow their harvest
So the wicked will turn and repent

cards.text: Then the song turns into a prayer to the LORD about people who are good and upright in heart. Upright, friend? My first years in that junk drawer I wasn't upright in ANYTHING; I was face-down in the dust.

cards.question: What does the psalm ask the LORD to do for those who are good and upright in heart?

cards.text: Then the flip side: some people take a turn. And it's the kind of turn where even the GPS stops talking and just sighs.

cards.question: Those who turn to ___ ways, the LORD will banish with the evildoers.

cards.text: And the very last line is a blessing: "Peace be upon Israel." Five verses, friend, and that little song stands like a MOUNTAIN, which is more than I can say for me on my tiptoes with the hat on.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "foreign" can be argued as right. In Scripture, turning to foreign ways is something the LORD judges, so a baker could defend "Those who turn to foreign ways, the LORD will banish with the evildoers." Replace it with a word that is clearly not the meaning of the line.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: The question says "those who are good," and only the right answer, "Do good to them," repeats the word "good." That echo makes the right answer stand out from "Give them long life" and "Make their names great."

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: The closing joke doesn't land. "That little song stands like a MOUNTAIN, which is more than I can say for me on my tiptoes with the hat on" leaves a reader asking "huh?": Papa Dorin stands on a gold base and has no tiptoes. The joke also moves the psalm's mountain picture from the people who trust the LORD onto the song itself, which blends the comparison with the Bible image.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.
